common_name: Lizard Lick Hosta (Narrow Spiky Medium Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Bred by R. Franks and Bob Solberg and registered in 2007 from a cross of H. 'Pineapple Pole' and H. rectifolia 'Aurea', Lizard Lick is a medium-sized hosta grown for its narrow, spiky, heavily rippled medium green leaves of good substance, each blade only about 7 inches long and 1 inch wide. It produces lavender flowers in late July and forms a mounded clump roughly 18 inches tall and 36 inches wide at maturity. Its upright, spiky-leaved habit reads as a distinctive textural accent among broader-leaved hostas, and it has also been used as a parent in later hosta breeding, including the large, grey-streaked cultivar Wildest Dreams. Grow in humus-rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

common_name: Woolman's Glory Chrysanthemum (Bronze Single-Flowered Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, pinching once in late spring to build a bushier plant before flower buds set.

directions: A long-grown single-flowered garden chrysanthemum classed among the late singles, Woolman's Glory produces bronze daisy-form blooms with a darker central disc on tall, roughly 4-foot stems, flowering in midseason into October alongside asters and ornamental grasses. Its reliable bronze coloring and classic single form made it popular enough to spawn several color sports that are still grown today, including the golden-flowered 'Golden Woolman's Glory'. Support the tall stems with discreet staking or grow-through netting, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous.
sources: British National Register of Chrysanthemum Names
